title: CSC3710 Sept 22, 2026: Regular expressions, identities, and DFAs

questions.q: Which regular expression over {a, b} describes exactly the strings of length less than 3?
questions.explain: List the lengths one at a time: length 0 (λ), length 1 (a ∪ b), and length 2 ((a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)). If you leave out λ, you lose the empty string. (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)(a ∪ b) gives exactly length 3, and (a ∪ b)*(a ∪ b)(a ∪ b) gives length 2 or more.

questions.q: Which regular expression over {a, b} describes exactly the strings of length greater than 3?
questions.explain: Greater than 3 means at least 4. Require four symbols, then allow anything after them. Without the trailing star you get exactly length 4. With only three fixed symbols you get length 3 or more. Starring the block of four gives lengths 0, 4, 8, and so on.

questions.q: Which regular expressions describe exactly the set of strings over {a, b} that contain the substring ab and have length greater than 2?
choices: (a ∪ b)*ab(a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)* ∪ (a ∪ b)*(a ∪ b)ab(a ∪ b)*
questions.explain: The ab needs at least one more symbol, either before it or after it. The first two options both say this: one uses four 3-symbol cases, and the other uses two cases (a symbol after ab, or a symbol before ab). (a ∪ b)*ab(a ∪ b)* also includes ab itself, which has length 2. The last option requires a symbol both before AND after ab, so it misses strings such as aba and abb, which belong in the set.

questions.q: Which regular expression describes exactly the strings over {a, b} of length 2 or more in which all a's precede all b's?
questions.explain: a⁺b⁺ covers strings with at least one a followed by at least one b, but it misses all-a and all-b strings such as aa and bb. aaa* and bbb* add those back while keeping length at least 2. a*b* wrongly includes λ, a, and b. (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)a*b* allows ba, where a b comes before an a.

questions.q: Give a string of length 2 that belongs to 'strings over {a, b} of length 2 or more in which all a's precede all b's' but is NOT generated by a⁺b⁺.
questions.explain: a⁺b⁺ requires at least one a and at least one b. The strings aa and bb meet the description (no a comes after a b), but they are missing from a⁺b⁺. That is why aaa* ∪ bbb* must be added.

questions.q: Regular expressions are built from alphabet symbols, λ, and ∅. Which of the following is NOT one of the operations used to build them?
questions.explain: Regular expressions use only union, concatenation, and Kleene star, with parentheses for grouping. u⁺ is just shorthand for uu*. An expression that uses any other operation is not a regular expression.

questions.q: Each regular set has exactly one correct regular expression.
questions.explain: One set can be described by many regular expressions. For example, 'contains ab and has length > 2' can be written with four 3-symbol cases or with two cases, and both are correct.

questions.q: Choose the regular set(s) over {a, b} to which the string abba belongs.
questions.explain: (a ∪ ab)*: no. Every b comes right after an a, so bb can never appear. (a ∪ b)*ab: no. Every string ends in b, and abba ends in a. The five-factor expression: no. Every string has length 5, and abba has length 4. (a ∪ ab)*ba: yes. Split it as ab · ba. (a ∪ b)*bb(a ∪ b)*: yes. Split it as a · bb · a.

questions.q: Choose the regular set(s) over {a, b} to which the string baab belongs.
questions.explain: (a ∪ b)*aa(a ∪ b)*: yes, as b · aa · b. (ba)*: no. Its nonempty strings end in a, and baab ends in b. b(a ∪ b)*b: yes, because it starts and ends with b and has aa in the middle. (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)(a ∪ b): no. Every string has length 3, and baab has length 4. (b ∪ aa)*: yes, using the blocks b, aa, b.

questions.q: The string abba belongs to (ab)*.
questions.explain: Strings in (ab)* repeat a, b over and over, so they never contain bb. Also, every nonempty string in (ab)* ends in b, and abba ends in a.

questions.q: The empty string λ belongs to (ab)*.
questions.explain: Kleene star always allows zero repetitions, so λ is in every starred set.

questions.q: The string aab belongs to (a ∪ ab)*.
questions.explain: Cut it into building blocks: a · ab. Both blocks are in {a, ab}, so aab is in {a, ab}*.

questions.q: Which string is NOT in the set described by b*(a ∪ λ)b*?
questions.explain: b*(a ∪ λ)b* gives some b's, then optionally one a, then some b's. Its strings contain at most one a. aba has two a's. bbb uses λ in the middle, bab uses a, and λ uses zero b's on both sides and λ in the middle.

questions.q: What is the quickest correct reason that abba is NOT in (a ∪ b)*ab?
choices: Every string in the set ends in b, but abba ends in a.
Every string in the set has length 2, but abba has length 4.
abba contains bb, which the set cannot produce.
questions.explain: Find a property that every string in the set has and that abba lacks. Here that property is the last symbol. The set contains strings longer than 2, and (a ∪ b)* can produce bb, so the length and bb reasons are wrong. Starting with a is allowed.

questions.q: For any regular expression u, what does ∅u equal?
questions.explain: Concatenation takes one string from each set. The empty set has no strings to take, so no strings can be formed: ∅u = u∅ = ∅.

questions.q: What does ∅* equal?
questions.explain: ∅⁰ = {λ}, and every higher power of ∅ is empty. Their union is {λ}, so ∅* = λ.

questions.q: (u ∪ v)w = wu ∪ wv is a valid identity for all regular expressions u, v, w.
questions.explain: Concatenation is not commutative. When you distribute from the right, w stays on the right: (u ∪ v)w = uw ∪ vw.

questions.q: Which of the following are valid identities for ALL regular expressions u, v, w?
questions.explain: u ∪ u = u holds because repeated elements don't matter. u* = (u*)* holds because starring again adds nothing new. λ* = λ holds. u(v ∪ w) = uv ∪ uw holds, with u staying on the left. uv = vu fails, since ab ≠ ba. u ∪ λ = u fails: with u = a, {a, λ} ≠ {a}. (u ∪ v)* = u* ∪ v* fails: ab is in (a ∪ b)* but not in a* ∪ b*.

questions.q: Use identities to simplify ∅a ∪ λb.
questions.explain: ∅a = ∅ and λb = b, which gives ∅ ∪ b. Then ∅ ∪ b = b ∪ ∅ (union is commutative) = b (u ∪ ∅ = u).

questions.q: Use identities to rewrite a(b ∪ λ) without parentheses, in simplest form.
questions.explain: a(b ∪ λ) = ab ∪ aλ by distributing from the left, and aλ = a by λu = uλ = u. The result is ab ∪ a.

questions.q: Why does u* = (u*)* hold?
choices: Any concatenation of strings from u* is already in u*, so starring again adds nothing new.
It only holds when u is a single alphabet symbol.
questions.explain: For example, {a, b}* already contains every concatenation of a's and b's. Gluing strings of {a, b}* together gives strings that are already in {a, b}*. The identity holds for every regular expression u.

questions.q: In the regular expression identities, u, v, and w must be single alphabet symbols.
questions.explain: u, v, and w can be any regular expressions, no matter how complicated. In proofs you often treat a whole subexpression, such as b*ab*, as one u or v.

questions.q: Apply u(v ∪ w) = uv ∪ uw to b*(a ∪ λ). Which result and substitution is correct?
choices: b*a ∪ b*λ, with u = b*, v = a, w = λ
ab* ∪ λb*, with u = b*, v = a, w = λ
b*a ∪ λ, with u = b*, v = a, w = λ
(b* ∪ a)(b* ∪ λ), with u = b*, v = a, w = λ
questions.explain: Distributing from the left keeps u = b* on the left of each term: b*a ∪ b*λ. Swapping the order is wrong because concatenation is not commutative.

questions.q: Apply (u ∪ v)w = uw ∪ vw to (b*a ∪ b*)b*. What do you get?
questions.explain: With u = b*a, v = b*, and w = b*, append w on the right of each term: b*a·b* ∪ b*·b*. Putting w on the left (b*b*a) is wrong because order matters.

questions.q: Apply (u* ∪ v)* = (u ∪ v)* to (b* ∪ b*ab*)*, using u = b and v = b*ab*. What do you get?
questions.explain: The identity drops the star on u = b, which is a whole member of the union under the outer star. The stars inside b*ab* each cover only part of v, so they stay. The outer star stays too.

questions.q: Using (u* ∪ v)* = (u ∪ v)*, the expression (b ∪ b*ab*)* can be rewritten as (b ∪ bab)*.
questions.explain: You can drop a star only when it covers an entire member of the union (the whole u). In b*ab* the stars cover only parts. The two sets also really are different: a is in (b ∪ b*ab*)* (take zero b's on each side), but a is not in (b ∪ bab)*.

questions.q: Using (u*v)*u* = (u ∪ v)* with u = b and v = a, what does (b*a)*b* become?
questions.explain: (b*a)*b* matches (u*v)*u* exactly when u = b and v = a, so it equals (b ∪ a)*. One more use of union commutativity turns this into (a ∪ b)*.

questions.q: Which of the following are sound practices when proving a regular expression equality with identities?
choices: Start from the more complicated side and simplify it until it matches the other side.
Rewrite both sides until they reach the same expression.
Generate a few strings from each side, and if they match, conclude that the expressions are equal.
At each step, name the identity used and what u, v, w stand for.
questions.explain: Simplifying the complicated side, or working on both sides until they meet, are both valid proofs as long as you justify each step with a named identity and its substitution. Checking a few sample strings is not a proof, because the sets are infinite.

questions.q: b*b* = b*
questions.explain: Concatenating two strings of b's gives a string of b's, so b*b* ⊆ b*. Any string w in b* can be written as w·λ with λ ∈ b*, so b* ⊆ b*b*. This step was used twice in the proof that (b*(a ∪ λ)b*)* = (a ∪ b)*.

questions.q: In a DFA M = (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F), what is the type of the transition function δ?
questions.explain: δ takes a state and an input symbol (an element of the Cartesian product Q × Σ) and returns a state. For example, δ(25¢, quarter) = 50¢.

questions.q: How many components (parts of the tuple) make up the formal definition of a DFA?
questions.explain: M = (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F): states, alphabet, transition function, initial state, and final states.

questions.q: A DFA must have at least one final state.
questions.explain: The only constraint is F ⊆ Q. The empty set is a subset of every set, so F = ∅ is allowed. This is similar to how a language is allowed to be empty.

questions.q: A DFA may have every one of its states marked final.
questions.explain: Every set is a subset of itself, so F = Q satisfies F ⊆ Q.

questions.q: A DFA may have two initial states.
questions.explain: The definition names exactly one initial state, q0 ∈ Q, marked with an arrow tip in the diagram. A diagram with no initial-state arrow is not a proper finite automaton.

questions.q: A DFA has 4 states and alphabet Σ = {0, 1, 2}. How many transition arrows does its state diagram have (count each self-loop as one arrow)?
questions.explain: δ is a function on Q × Σ, so every (state, symbol) pair has exactly one arrow: |Q| × |Σ| = 4 × 3 = 12.

questions.q: A DFA can get stuck on an input symbol if some state has no outgoing arrow for that symbol.
questions.explain: δ is a total function: every state has exactly one outgoing arrow for every symbol. A DFA never gets stuck, although an arrow may loop back to the same state.

questions.q: What constraint does the DFA definition place on the set of final states F?
choices: F and Q must be disjoint
questions.explain: The only requirement is that F is a subset of Q. It can be anything from ∅ up to Q.

questions.q: When a DFA is viewed as a language acceptor, what does it mean if the machine finishes reading a string in a final state?
questions.explain: As language acceptors, machines either accept or reject a string. Ending in a final (accepting) state means the string is accepted.

questions.q: The vending-machine DFA has states $0, 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, and '$1 or more', and inputs q (quarter) and h (half-dollar). What is δ(50¢, h)?
questions.explain: 50¢ plus a half-dollar makes $1.00, so the machine moves to '$1 or more'.

questions.q: In the vending-machine DFA (states $0, 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, '$1 or more'; inputs q = quarter, h = half-dollar), what is δ(25¢, h)?
In the vending-machine DFA, δ(75¢, h) = '$1 or more', even though 75¢ + 50¢ is more than $1.
questions.explain: Any total of $1 or more lands in the '$1 or more' state, including overpayment. That is why the state has that name.

questions.q: How many entries does the transition table of the vending-machine DFA have (5 states, inputs quarter and half-dollar)?
questions.explain: The table has one row per state and one column per symbol, so there are |Q| × |Σ| = 5 × 2 = 10 entries, one for each value δ(state, symbol).

questions.q: In the vending-machine DFA, starting in $0, the inputs quarter, quarter, half-dollar are read in that order. Which state is the machine in at the end?
questions.explain: $0 goes to 25¢ on a quarter, then to 50¢ on a quarter, then to '$1 or more' on a half-dollar.

questions.q: In the vending machine, the '$1 or more' state releases a bottle and resets the counter to 0. What is δ($1 or more, quarter)?
questions.explain: After the reset, the next coin counts from zero, so a quarter leads to 25¢. The machine never goes back into the $0 state itself. $0 is only where it starts.

questions.q: Why is it a bad design to make $0 the final state of the vending machine (and drop the '$1 or more' state)?
choices: The machine starts in $0, so it would release a bottle as soon as it was plugged in.
A DFA's initial state is never allowed to be final.
A DFA must have at least two final states.
questions.explain: In this machine the final state means 'release a bottle'. If $0 were final, plugging the machine in would release a free bottle, and so would unplugging it and plugging it back in. The definition does allow the initial state to be final (F ⊆ Q is the only constraint). It is just a poor design here.
